title: Periphrastic constructions and the perfect

objectives.can: Recognise εἰμί with a participle as one verbal expression and name the tense it stands for.

explanation.summary: Greek can build a tense out of two words: a form of εἰμί, 'to be', and a participle. ἦν διδάσκων is, roughly, an imperfect: 'he was teaching'. ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι is, roughly, a perfect. Reading the two words as one expression keeps you from translating the participle as a separate circumstance.

sections.heading: Two words, one verb
body: A periphrastic construction (from a Greek word for 'speaking around') uses a form of εἰμί together with a participle that agrees with the subject. Luke 4:31 says ἦν διδάσκων αὐτοὺς ἐν τοῖς σάββασιν. The verb ἦν is imperfect, third person singular, and διδάσκων is a present participle, nominative singular masculine. Together they say that he was teaching them on the sabbaths.

The participle carries the meaning of the action, and the form of εἰμί carries person, number, mood and, mostly, the time. So the pair does the work of one verb. In Luke 4:31 it does what the simple imperfect ἐδίδασκεν does in Luke 4:15.

sections.heading: Which tense does the pair stand for?
body: The tense of εἰμί fixes the time frame, and the tense of the participle adds how the action is seen. A present participle gives the ongoing or repeated view; a perfect participle gives a state that results from an earlier action. This is the usual reading, and the table below shows the combinations most often met.

Do not treat the table as a translation machine. The periphrastic form and the simple tense are close in meaning, but writers choose between them, and grammarians disagree about how much the choice adds. Some say that the periphrastic form stresses a continuing activity or a state; others think it is often only a style of the writer. Test each example in its passage.

head: Form of εἰμί + participle
Stands for
Example
rows: ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν, Luke 5:10; ἔσεσθε μισούμενοι, Matthew 10:22
perfect: has done, and the result stands
pluperfect: had done, and the result stood
future perfect: will have been done

sections.heading: The perfect with εἰμί
body: The perfect participle describes a state. So ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι in Ephesians 2:8 says that the readers are in the condition of having been saved. The word order may be turned round, as in Hebrews 10:10, where the participle comes first: ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμέν, 'we are ones who have been made holy'. In John 3:24, ἦν βεβλημένος is the same pattern in the past: John 'had been thrown' into prison, and the sentence says he was not yet in that state.

For some verbs the third person plural of the perfect or pluperfect middle and passive was an awkward form, and writers often used the participle with εἰμί instead. You will meet this in forms like ἦσαν συνηγμένοι. Take it as a tendency in the grammars, not as a rule for every verb.

sections.heading: Not every εἰμί with a participle is periphrastic
body: Three checks help. First, the article: in John 4:26, Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ λαλῶν σοι, the participle has the article, so it is a noun phrase: 'I am the one who is speaking to you'. Second, a separate predicate: in Ephesians 2:10, ἐσμεν ποίημα already has its complement, so κτισθέντες after the comma is a circumstance and not part of the verb. Third, sense: if the participle is plainly an adjective for a lasting quality, as with the perfect participles of many verbs, it is hard to say whether the pair is a tense or a verb with a predicate adjective.

That last case is a real boundary, and the grammars draw it in different places. For this lesson, count the pair as a tense when the participle describes an action or state of the subject and nothing else in the clause serves as the predicate.

sections.heading: Where you meet it
body: The construction turns up in many New Testament books, but it is especially frequent in Luke and Acts: ἦν διδάσκων appears in Luke 4:31, 5:17, 13:10 and 19:47. Luke 5:17 gives three examples in one verse.

Reading it as one expression changes the translation. ἦν διδάσκων is 'was teaching' or 'used to teach', not 'he was, teaching'. The pair often sets a scene or describes a habit, and then other verbs move the story on.

misunderstandings: Translating the two words separately, as 'he was' and 'teaching'. The pair is one verb; the participle is not an adverbial circumstance here.
Reading the perfect participle as a past action only. ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι stresses the state in which the readers now are.
Taking every εἰμί beside a participle as periphrastic. Check for the article and for a separate predicate.
Assuming that the periphrastic form always means something different from the simple tense. The two overlap, and the writer's choice is sometimes a matter of style.

deeper.heading: Semitic colouring?
body: Many examples in Luke and Acts have been explained as the influence of Aramaic, where a similar pattern is common, or of the Greek Old Testament, which translates Hebrew. Other scholars point out that Greek had such constructions long before the New Testament, especially for the perfect, and that Luke could have written them without a Semitic model. The question is argued and the evidence allows both views; a reader does not need to settle it to read the Greek.

deeper.heading: The future perfect
body: The pair ἔσται δεδεμένον in Matthew 16:19 is a future perfect in form: 'will have been bound'. Translators and commentators differ on whether it means that heaven's act follows the earthly act or that the earthly act matches something already settled. That is a question of interpretation, and the grammar alone does not decide it.

examples.analysis: ἦν is the imperfect of εἰμί, third person singular, and διδάσκων is a present active participle, nominative singular masculine, agreeing with the subject, Jesus, who has just gone down to Capernaum. The pair stands for the imperfect: 'he was teaching them on the sabbaths'. The sentence says what he was doing there, and the sentence before it brings him to Capernaum.

examples.analysis: ἔσται is the future of εἰμί and δεδεμένον and λελυμένον are perfect passive participles in the neuter singular, agreeing with ὅ, 'whatever'. Each pair stands for a future perfect, 'will have been bound' and 'will have been loosed'. How to translate and understand the pair is a matter of interpretation; the point here is that the form is a tense made of two words.

examples.analysis: This looks like a periphrastic form, but it is not one. ἐσμεν already has its complement in ποίημα, 'a work', and the participle κτισθέντες follows the comma as a circumstance: 'we are his work, created in Christ Jesus'. A periphrastic expression would have no other predicate.

options: The imperfect: 'he was teaching'
The perfect: 'he has taught'
The aorist: 'he taught once'

practice.explain: ἦν is imperfect and διδάσκων is a present participle, so the pair gives the ongoing view in past time. It is much like the simple imperfect ἐδίδασκεν.

options: The present: 'you catch'
The pluperfect: 'you had caught'
The future: 'you will be catching people'
The imperfect: 'you were catching'
practice.explain: ἔσῃ is the future of εἰμί, second person singular, and ζωγρῶν is a present participle agreeing with the 'you'. The pair is a future with an ongoing sense, and ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν points forward from this moment.

practice.explain: ἐστε is present and σεσῳσμένοι is a perfect participle. A present form of εἰμί with a perfect participle stands for the perfect: a state that results from an earlier act.

options: As a purpose clause: 'he was in order to teach'
As a genitive absolute
As one verb, an imperfect: 'he was teaching'
As two verbs: 'he was' and 'he teaches'
check.explain: A form of εἰμί and a participle agreeing with the subject make one periphrastic verb. Here it is imperfect, and the scene it sets is a sabbath in a synagogue. The participle is nominative, so no genitive absolute is possible.

options: ἦσαν is imperfect, third plural, and πορευόμενοι agrees with the subject: 'two of them were travelling'
ἦσαν πορευόμενοι is a future: 'they will go'
πορευόμενοι is genitive and belongs to κώμην
ἦσαν is aorist and πορευόμενοι is a noun
check.explain: ἦσαν is the imperfect of εἰμί, third plural. πορευόμενοι is a present middle participle in the nominative plural, agreeing with δύο. The pair stands for the imperfect of πορεύομαι.

The perfect: 'you have been hated'
The aorist passive: 'you were hated'
check.explain: ἔσεσθε is the future of εἰμί, second plural, and μισούμενοι is a present passive participle. The pair is a future passive with an ongoing sense. ὑπὸ πάντων names those who do the hating.

Jerusalem is trampling now and always
Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations
Jerusalem will trample the nations

options: ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμέν: an imperfect, 'we were being made holy'
θελήματι ἐσμέν: a future
ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμέν: a perfect, 'we have been made holy', with the participle first
No pair is periphrastic, because the participle comes first
check.explain: A perfect participle with a present form of εἰμί stands for the perfect, and the order of the two words is free. A participle before εἰμί is no less periphrastic.

options: That Aeneas was in the condition of having been paralysed: a pluperfect state
That Aeneas will be paralysed
That Aeneas is the one who is paralysing
That Aeneas paralysed someone
check.explain: ὃς is the relative pronoun, 'who', and ἦν παραλελυμένος is an imperfect of εἰμί with a perfect passive participle. The pair stands for the pluperfect: he was in a state of paralysis, which began earlier.

options: The imperfect: 'who kept coming'
The present: 'who come'
The pluperfect: 'who had come' from all the villages, and were there
The future: 'who will come'
check.explain: ἦσαν is imperfect and ἐληλυθότες is a perfect active participle, nominative plural, agreeing with the relative οἵ. The pair stands for the pluperfect. Earlier in the verse ἦν διδάσκων is a periphrastic imperfect.

check.prompt: αὐτοῦ γάρ ἐσμεν ποίημα, κτισθέντες ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Is ἐσμεν … κτισθέντες (words 2 and 4) a periphrastic verb?

options: Yes: a perfect, because the participle is passive
Yes: any εἰμί with a participle is periphrastic
No: because κτισθέντες is in the genitive
No: ἐσμεν has its own complement ποίημα, and κτισθέντες adds a circumstance
check.explain: A periphrastic expression uses the participle as the main part of the verb. Here ποίημα already completes ἐσμεν, so κτισθέντες is an adverbial or attributive participle after it. It is also aorist, not perfect.

check.prompt: λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ λαλῶν σοι. How does the participle λαλῶν (word 7) work?

Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It is a noun phrase with the article: 'I am the one speaking to you'
It forms an imperfect with εἰμι: 'I was speaking'
It is in the genitive and belongs to σοι
It forms a future with εἰμι: 'I will speak'
check.explain: The article ὁ makes λαλῶν a substantival participle: 'the one who is speaking'. It is the predicate of Ἐγώ εἰμι, not part of a tense. εἰμι is present.

check.prompt: Luke and Acts have many examples of εἰμί with a participle. Which statement about this is the soundest?

options: Some scholars see Semitic influence, others note that Greek already had the pattern; the question is argued
It always has a different meaning from the simple tense
It occurs only in Luke and nowhere else in Greek
It proves that Luke could not write ordinary Greek
check.explain: The pattern is found in earlier Greek, especially for the perfect, and is also common in Aramaic and in the Greek translation of the Old Testament. Scholars weigh these differently. Neither view is a reason to say that Luke wrote poor Greek, and the periphrastic and the simple tense overlap in meaning.
